newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Katangans try to bury Zaire past, make fresh start.
newsitem.headline: Katangans try to bury Zaire past, make fresh start.

text.p: "Welcome to Congo" reads the inscription at the Kasumbalesa border post -- gateway to the Zairean province of Katanga from Zambia to the south.
"Welcome to Congo" says the immigration clerk, practising his English with sudden urgency in a gesture symbolic of a break with 100 years of francophone dominance.
He apologises that his visa stamp still says Zaire but promises that within days his new masters will give him one in the name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
"Now we have to build our country from scratch, make a fresh start. Now we will learn to speak English because those French, they really messed us up," he adds.

In Lubumbashi, current headquarters of the newly declared government of Laurent Kabila, the old Zairean flag has disappeared and it is the flag of the rebel alliance -- sky blue with seven yellow stars -- that flies on public buildings.

The people of Lubumbashi say they are intent on forgetting 30 years of rule by Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator widely denounced as a corrupt thief who fled the capital Kinshasa on Friday and lost the city to Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) one day later.

Kabila, one of the few politicians untainted by association with Mobutu, appears immensely popular in Lubumbashi, not least because he is from the local Luba people and this was his home province until he went east to hatch revolution.
"Everyone is very happy," said Christophe, a small-time trader who carries goods to and fro across the Zambian border.
"Prices have gone down since Kabila came, chicken, tomatoes, onions, everything, you name it," he added, echoing a widespread impression which no one can fully explain.

The new zaire, a currency that was the laughing stock of Africa because of rampant inflation, has won a lease of life, almost doubling in value in less than a month. It now stands at 140,000 to the dollar, from a low of 250,000.
"It's because the banks have lots of hard currency. Money has been pouring into the region. People can buy dollars from the bank at the official rate," said a shopkeeper.

For the copper and cobalt mining industry, the mainstay of the local economy, it is largely business as usual, with the difference that investors hope the new rulers can cut out some of the corruption that made life so trying under Mobutu.
One mining manager said his company made a seamless transition from the Mobutu government to Kabila's people.
In a clear sign of confidence in the new order, the company is pressing ahead with plans to invest more than $200 million in the Tenke and Fungurume mines northwest of Lubumbashi.
"The company came to the conclusion that Kabila was going to be in charge. They turned out to be right," he said.

On the political front, Kabila's arrival has buried the ghost of Katangan separatism -- a chronic thorn in the flesh for Mobutu, who came from a northern region about 2,000 km (1,200 miles) away from Lubumbashi.

On Saturday the sons of former Katangan gendarmes who fled to Angola in 1963 after a first attempt at secession were limbering up at a recruitment barracks in the city, in readiness for integration into a new national army.
The exiles have helped Kabila's forces in their campaign to seize national power in Kinshasa -- another illustration of the shift in power between the regions.
Alliance officials say Kabila is even thinking of making Lubumbashi the capital, at least for a transitional period.
Residents welcome the prestige and business that would bring them but wonder if the city really has the infrastructure to play host to an effective national government.
One cloud on the horizon, a potential source of trouble down the road, is the widespread belief that the alliance forces include many soldiers of Rwandan and Ugandan origin.
"The AFDL people tell us that they will all go home when the war is over. But people are worried that they won't," said a local politician who asked not to be named.
"That could cause problems," he added.
